Expectations connect a probability distribution to an average quantity of interest.
Jensen’s inequality compares transformations of those averages, while Monte Carlo estimation approximates them from samples.
This distinction matters whenever a desired average, such as expected prediction loss, is defined over a distribution but only sampled observations are available.

## Expectation of a function {#expectation}

An expectation is a distribution-weighted average of a random quantity.
Let $X$ have probability mass function $p$, and let $f(X)$ be the numerical quantity being averaged.
For a discrete variable,

$$
  \mathbb E_p[f(X)]=\sum_x p(x)f(x).
$$

For a real variable with density $p$, replace the sum with an integral:

$$
  \mathbb E_p[f(X)]=\int f(x)p(x)\,dx.
$$

Assume the relevant expectation exists; [absolute integrability]{.term key="absolute-integrability"} gives a finite expectation.
Choosing $f(x)=x$ gives the mean, while choosing a loss or a log probability gives the corresponding expected objective.
The expectation is determined by the distribution; an observed sample average is an estimator of it.
See [Deep Learning, Section 3.8](https://www.deeplearningbook.org/contents/prob.html) for expectation and variance.

## Jensen’s inequality {#jensen}

For [convex]{.term key="convex-function"} $f$, Jensen's inequality states $f(\mathbb E[X])\leq\mathbb E[f(X)]$, provided the expectations exist.
The inequality reverses for concave functions, including $\ln$.
This is the mechanism behind a variational lower bound on log evidence.
For a differentiable convex function, a supporting tangent line gives a short proof; Jensen's inequality itself also applies to nondifferentiable convex functions.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Proof: Jensen's inequality for differentiable convex functions"}

Let $m=\mathbb E[X]$ lie in the function's domain and assume the displayed expectations are finite.
Convexity implies that the tangent line at $m$ lies below the graph:

$$
  f(x)\geq f(m)+f'(m)(x-m).
$$

Taking expectations on both sides gives

$$
  \begin{aligned}
  \mathbb E[f(X)]
  &\geq f(m)+f'(m)(\mathbb E[X]-m)\\
  &=f(m).
  \end{aligned}
$$

The linear term vanishes by the definition of $m$.
For a concave function, apply the same argument to its convex negative and reverse the inequality.
The [subgradient definition](optimization.qmd#subgradients) generalises the supporting-line idea beyond ordinary derivatives.

:::

[The ELBO](elbo.qmd#deriving-the-bound) applies the concave-log form to latent-variable evidence.
[KL divergence](entropy.qmd#kl-divergence) uses the convex function $-\ln$ to establish nonnegativity.

## Monte Carlo sample averages {#monte-carlo}

To estimate $\mathbb E_q[f(X)]$, draw $L$ independent samples $X^{(l)}\sim q$ and average $f$ on those samples:

$$
  \widehat\mu_L=\frac1L\sum_{l=1}^L f(X^{(l)}).
$$

Under finite [variance]{.term key="variance"}, this estimator is unbiased and its variance is $\operatorname{Var}_q(f(X))/L$.
The function being averaged need not itself be a probability.
VAE training commonly uses Monte Carlo estimates of expectations over latent noise, with a [reparameterised sample](reparameterization.qmd) to obtain a pathwise gradient.
Random sampling does not categorically forbid gradients; the estimator and dependence on parameters determine how to differentiate.

## An average before or after squaring {#example}

Let $X$ equal $-1$ or $1$ with equal probabilities, and take $f(x)=x^2$.
Then $\mathbb E[X]=0$, so $(\mathbb E[X])^2=0$, while $\mathbb E[X^2]=1$.
The mean cancels opposite signs; the mean square retains their magnitude.
This is a concrete instance of Jensen's inequality and explains why a mean residual can vanish while mean squared error remains positive.

A sample average of $X$ can fluctuate around zero, but every sample average of $X^2$ in this example is exactly one.
The target expectation is a fixed number once the distribution and function are specified; a Monte Carlo estimator is a random quantity before its samples are drawn.
Increasing the number of independent samples reduces sampling variance, but it does not correct sampling from the wrong distribution.

## Estimating a latent reconstruction term {#latent-expectation}

For a [CVAE](../machine-learning/autoencoders.qmd#conditioning), let $A$ be an observed example, $o$ its context, and $z^{(l)}$ independent draws from the encoder $q_\phi(z\mid A,o)$.
An expectation over the encoder can be estimated with $L$ independent latent samples:

$$
  \widehat R=-\frac1L\sum_{l=1}^{L}
  \log p_\theta(A\mid o,z^{(l)}).
$$

The factor $1/L$ averages latent samples; an additional minibatch average accounts for training examples.
Using one sample per example is a Monte Carlo estimator, not an assertion that the posterior is deterministic. [VAE, §§2.2–2.4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1312.6114#page=3).

## Connections {#connections}

[Probability](probability.qmd) distinguishes random variables, values, masses, densities, and conditioning.
[Reparameterisation](reparameterization.qmd) lets suitable Monte Carlo samples carry pathwise gradients and gives a training implementation.
[The ELBO](elbo.qmd) identifies the reconstruction expectation being estimated, while [Gaussian KL](entropy.qmd#gaussian-kl) can be calculated analytically.
